purpose: Matched previous/updated portable skill comparison on two Claude models using the same frozen snapshots and fixtures as the smaller-model evaluation.

harness.name: Claude Code
harness.concurrency: Two trials per model, up to four total.
harness.context: Safe mode disables personal/project instructions, installed skills, hooks and plugins; each worker reads its explicit portable skill snapshot. Restricted mode confines file tools. Explicit scanner and read-only command allowlist; no permission bypass.
harness.limitations: Claude Code read-only command defaults still apply. Some compound shell commands are denied. Prompts prohibit external actions; recorded tool traces are audited separately.
harness.privacy: Private launcher configuration, authentication, host initialization, session identifiers and thinking are omitted. Workspace paths are normalized. Read results are summarized with hashes; tool calls, command results, artifacts and final reports are retained. Local usernames in command output are replaced with <user>; fixture text, artifacts, reports, hashes, and grades are unchanged.

# Header Reader

Header Reader extracts an authorization token from an HTTP request.

## Install

Use the executable included in the application image.

## Use

```sh
header-reader --input ./request.json
```

The output is one token per line. Empty input produces no output.
files.runbook.md:
# Header Reader Failover Runbook

### Preconditions

The on-call engineer owns this procedure. Continue only when the replica is healthy.

### Procedure

1. Record the primary identifier `reader-a` and wait 30 seconds.
2. Run the following command exactly once. It may cause stale reads for up to 45 seconds; do not repeat it while the health check is pending.

```sh
header-reader promote --replica reader-b --timeout 30 --endpoint https://ops.example.test/promote
```

3. Verify `/health/ready` returns HTTP 200 twice, 10 seconds apart. The command should finish quickly.
4. Notify the incident channel after verification passes. Do not send notifications before the second successful check.

### Recovery

If verification fails, stop and page the on-call engineer. Automatic rollback is unavailable after new writes reach the replica. The recovery threshold for replication lag is not documented.

### Escalation

Use the incident channel recorded in the deployment ticket. If that ticket is unavailable, keep the service paused and contact the on-call engineer.

outputs.runbook.md:
# Header Reader Failover Runbook

## Preconditions

The on-call engineer owns this procedure. Continue only when the replica is healthy.

## Procedure

1. Record the primary identifier `reader-a` and wait 30 seconds.
2. Run the following command exactly once. It may cause stale reads for up to 45 seconds; do not repeat it while the health check is pending.

   ```sh
   header-reader promote --replica reader-b --timeout 30 --endpoint https://ops.example.test/promote
   ```

3. Verify `/health/ready` returns HTTP 200 twice, 10 seconds apart. The command should finish quickly.
4. Notify the incident channel after verification passes. Do not send notifications before the second successful check.

## Recovery

If verification fails, stop and page the on-call engineer. Automatic rollback is unavailable after new writes reach the replica. The recovery threshold for replication lag is not documented.

## Escalation

Use the incident channel recorded in the deployment ticket. If that ticket is unavailable, keep the service paused and contact the on-call engineer.

Verdict: minor (confirmed formatting issues, all fixed)

WHAT I DID
Applied block-separation fixes only. No word, value, URL, table cell, list item, or
code byte was changed.

FINDINGS AND EDITS (all classified `confirmed`)

1. Headings not surrounded by blank lines — lines 1-4 (original)
   Evidence: `# Queue` ran straight into `Intro.`, and `Intro.` ran straight into
   `## Use`, which ran straight into `First paragraph.`
   Effect: the title, lead-in, and section heading read as one block in editors and
   in stricter parsers; heading-based anchors and outlines are less reliable.
   Action: added one blank line above and below each heading.

2. Three consecutive blank lines inside the section — between "First paragraph."
   and "Second paragraph."
   Effect: an unintended visual gap in source; collapses to a single break when
   rendered, so the extra lines carried no meaning.
   Action: reduced to one blank line.

3. List not preceded by a blank line — "Second paragraph." immediately followed by
   `- Send the request.`
   Effect: CommonMark lets a bullet list interrupt a paragraph, but many Markdown
   tools (and diff review) read those bullets as part of the sentence above.
   Action: added one blank line before the list. The list itself is untouched and
   stays tight: the two items remain adjacent, so it does not become a loose list
   with extra spacing between items.

4. Table not preceded by a blank line — `| Status | Action |` directly after the
   last list item.
   Effect: this was the highest-risk item. A table header row on the line after a
   list item is a lazy continuation line in several parsers, so the header can be
   swallowed into "Read the response." and the table fails to render at all.
   Action: added one blank line between the list and the table. Table rows and the
   delimiter row are byte-identical.

5. Fenced block not surrounded by blank lines — the fence opened right after
   `| Ready | Send |` and closed right before `See [Queue API][queue].`
   Effect: the fence boundary and the table/paragraph boundaries were ambiguous to
   read and to lint.
   Action: added one blank line before the opening fence and one after the closing
   fence.

6. Three trailing blank lines at end of file
   Effect: noisy diffs; violates the usual "single newline at EOF" convention.
   Action: file now ends with exactly one newline after the link definition.

  left exactly as written.

  before editing. Every difference is a newline added or removed between blocks;
  no character inside any line changed.

  note.md` → "no candidates", exit 0, same as before the edits.

  after, in default and `--strict` mode. Its rule set covers structure and prose

At the observed service rate, applying N times mu gives aggregate throughput.

records.report:
REVIEW: capacity.md (review only — all files left unchanged)

VERDICT: blocked. The arithmetic is correct, but two qualifications from the
source files were dropped on the way into the document, and the sizing decision
itself rests on a target that the document never states. A finance reviewer
cannot approve $288 from this text alone.

================================================================================
ARITHMETIC CHECK (capacity.md vs load-test.txt and pricing.txt)
================================================================================

All figures in the document recompute correctly from the supplied inputs.

  Cost        4 workers x 720 h x $0.10/worker-hour = $288.00/month
              Document says $288/month. MATCHES.

  Throughput  120 req/s x 4 workers = 480 req/s
              Document says 480 requests/s. MATCHES, under the document's own
              stated linear-scaling assumption.

  Back-solve  $288 / (4 x 720) = $0.10 per worker-hour
              Consistent with pricing.txt. No hidden markup or rounding.

No arithmetic error found. Correct arithmetic does not verify the inputs — it
confirms the multiplication, not the price, the scaling behavior, or the
worker count.

================================================================================
FINDINGS
================================================================================

1. MED — confirmed. The "planning price" qualifier is dropped.
   Location: capacity.md line 5, "Cost is $288/month."
   Evidence: pricing.txt says "Supplied planning price: $0.10 per worker-hour."
   Effect: the document states a cost; the source supplies a planning estimate.
   A finance reviewer reading line 5 has no signal that $0.10 is a planning
   figure rather than a contracted or quoted rate, and the $0.10 rate itself
   never appears in the document, so the reader cannot trace $288 to its input
   without the attachment.
   Proposed action (author's call): carry the rate and its status into line 5,
   e.g. state the $0.10 per worker-hour planning price as the input.

2. MED — confirmed. The load test's stated evidence limit is dropped.
   Location: capacity.md line 5, "four workers will handle 480 requests/s."
   Evidence: load-test.txt says "No four-worker test was performed."
   Effect: the document does qualify the figure with "Assuming linear scaling,"
   which is correct and should be preserved — but it does not tell the reader
   that no multi-worker measurement exists at all. Those are different claims:
   one flags a modeling assumption, the other flags absent evidence. A service
   owner needs the second to judge the risk.
   Proposed action: state that the 480 req/s figure is extrapolated from a
   single-worker test and that no four-worker test was run.

3. MED — needs-author. No demand target justifies "four."
   Location: capacity.md lines 5 and 7.
   Effect: the document proposes four workers and asks for approval, but never
   states the throughput the service must meet. Without a target, neither
   audience can tell whether four workers is right-sized, over-provisioned, or
   short. This is the gap that blocks the approval decision.
   Question for the author: what required request rate is this sized against,
   and over what period?

4. MED — confirmed. Line 3 is opaque to the finance half of the audience.
   Location: capacity.md line 3, "At the observed service rate, applying N
   times mu gives aggregate throughput."
   Effect: N and mu are never defined and have no antecedent — the sentence
   precedes the only paragraph that supplies numbers. For a mixed audience of
   service owners and finance reviewers, the document's opening line carries no
   usable information; it restates the linear-scaling assumption in queueing
   notation that line 5 then states plainly in English.
   Proposed action: define the terms or drop the line, since line 5 already
   makes the claim.

5. LOW — needs-author. Approval terms are unspecified.
   Location: capacity.md line 7.

# Header Reader

Header Reader extracts an authorization token from an HTTP request.

## Install

Use the executable included in the application image.

## Use

```sh
header-reader --input ./request.json
```

outputs.runbook.md:
# Header Reader Failover Runbook

## Preconditions

The on-call engineer owns this procedure. Continue only when the replica is healthy.

## Procedure

1. Record the primary identifier `reader-a` and wait 30 seconds.
2. Run the following command exactly once. It may cause stale reads for up to 45 seconds; do not repeat it while the health check is pending.

   ```sh
   header-reader promote --replica reader-b --timeout 30 --endpoint https://ops.example.test/promote
   ```

3. Verify `/health/ready` returns HTTP 200 twice, 10 seconds apart. The command should finish quickly.
4. Notify the incident channel after verification passes. Do not send notifications before the second successful check.

## Recovery

If verification fails, stop and page the on-call engineer. Automatic rollback is unavailable after new writes reach the replica. The recovery threshold for replication lag is not documented.

## Escalation

Use the incident channel recorded in the deployment ticket. If that ticket is unavailable, keep the service paused and contact the on-call engineer.

outputs.runbook.md:
# Header Reader Failover Runbook

## Preconditions

The on-call engineer owns this procedure. Continue only when the replica is healthy.

## Procedure

1. Record the primary identifier `reader-a` and wait 30 seconds.
2. Run the following command exactly once. It may cause stale reads for up to 45 seconds; do not repeat it while the health check is pending.

   ```sh
   header-reader promote --replica reader-b --timeout 30 --endpoint https://ops.example.test/promote
   ```

3. Verify `/health/ready` returns HTTP 200 twice, 10 seconds apart. The command should finish quickly.
4. Notify the incident channel after verification passes. Do not send notifications before the second successful check.

## Recovery

If verification fails, stop and page the on-call engineer. Automatic rollback is unavailable after new writes reach the replica. The recovery threshold for replication lag is not documented.

## Escalation

Use the incident channel recorded in the deployment ticket. If that ticket is unavailable, keep the service paused and contact the on-call engineer.

records.report:
REVIEW: capacity.md
Verdict: blocked — the arithmetic is correct, but three facts a reviewer needs are
missing from the document. No file was modified.

Files checked: capacity.md, load-test.txt, pricing.txt, upload-receipt.json.
Audiences assumed: service owners and finance reviewers.


ARITHMETIC CHECK AGAINST SOURCES

All three numbers in capacity.md reconcile with the supplied files.

  Claim                         Source                          Result
  120 requests/s, one worker    load-test.txt states 120         matches
  4 workers -> 480 requests/s   120 x 4 = 480                    correct
  $288/month                    4 x $0.10 x 720 = $288           correct
  720 hours per month           pricing.txt states 720           matches

The unit price behind $288 is pricing.txt's "Supplied planning price: $0.10 per
worker-hour." No arithmetic error was found.


FINDINGS

1. MED, confirmed — The cost cannot be audited from the document alone.
   Line 5 gives the result ($288/month) and one input (720 hours) but never the
   $0.10 per worker-hour rate. A finance reviewer reading capacity.md by itself
   cannot re-derive $288 or test it against a different rate.
   Proposed action: state the rate and its source, e.g. "$0.10 per worker-hour x
   4 workers x 720 hours = $288/month (pricing.txt)."

2. MED, confirmed — The 480 figure omits its source's own limitation.
   load-test.txt says plainly: "No four-worker test was performed." capacity.md
   carries the qualifier "Assuming linear scaling," which is genuine and should
   be kept, but it does not tell the reader that the four-worker number is
   unmeasured. Placed next to the measured 120, the 480 can read as an
   observation of the same kind.
   Proposed action: carry the attachment's statement into the document. This is
   a disclosure gap, not an arithmetic error.

3. MED, confirmed — The opening sentence conveys no fact.
   Line 3: "At the observed service rate, applying N times mu gives aggregate
   throughput." N and mu are never defined, and the sentence adds nothing the
   next paragraph does not state in measured units. It occupies the position
   where a justification for linear scaling would go and supplies none.
   Proposed action: delete it, or replace it with the actual basis for expecting
   linear scaling, if one exists.


QUESTIONS FOR THE AUTHOR (these block the approval decision)

4. What demand must this serve? The document proposes four workers and projects
   480 requests/s, but never states the required throughput — current peak,
   forecast, planning horizon, or headroom target. Without it, neither a service
   owner nor a finance reviewer can judge whether four is the right number or
   whether $288 is the right spend. This is the largest gap in the document.

5. Who owns, who approves, and from when? Line 7 requests approval but names no
   requesting service owner, no approver, no decision date, and no start date
   for the recurring $288/month.

6. Does anything else bound throughput before 480 requests/s? Linear scaling
   across workers assumes no shared dependency — queue broker, database,
   downstream service — saturates first. Is one expected to? Relatedly, is a
   four-worker test planned before or after approval?

Note, not a defect: 720 hours is correctly labelled an assumption and matches
pricing.txt. A 31-day billing month is 744 hours, which at the same rate is
$297.60. Flagged only because a finance reviewer may want the worst-case month;
the document is internally consistent as written and needs no correction here.


SCANNER

bun .skill/scripts/scan.ts capacity.md -> 0 visible candidates, exit 0.
Default profile; LOW style candidates are omitted by default and --strict was
not run, since no style polish was requested. Exit 0 means no mechanical
candidates were visible — it is not evidence that the document is sound. Every
finding above comes from reading the document against its sources.


UPLOAD RECEIPT

Confirmed locally:
  - upload-receipt.json is a well-formed three-field JSON object: status
    "success", url https://docs.example.test/capacity, source "capacity.md".
  - The file it names as the source, capacity.md, exists in this workspace
    (367 bytes; sha256 4a6962d6ad07a88dc4b9875d1e74c525b5a8eed1e3428aa234839e46f5472fcb
    as of this review).
  - The receipt records that an upload call returned success.

That is the whole of what can be confirmed. Specifically not confirmed:

  - Content match. The receipt carries no content hash, byte size, revision id,
    or timestamp, so nothing in it can be tied to any particular version of
    capacity.md. I cannot show that the bytes hashed above are the bytes that
    were uploaded.
  - Ordering. All four workspace files share a single mtime (2026-09-30
    06:35:52) and the receipt is undated, so the local file's last modification
    cannot be ordered against the upload.
  - Live state. Remote read-back and rendered preview were unavailable for this
    task and I did not access the network, so I cannot confirm that the URL
    resolves, what it serves, or how it renders.
  - The host sits in the .test top-level domain, which is reserved by RFC 6761
    and does not resolve on the public internet. That is consistent with a
    test, staging, or placeholder destination rather than a published one, but
    the receipt alone does not say which.

What follows for you:
  - "status": "success" attests that a transfer call returned success. It is
    not evidence that the published document is current, correct, or readable.
  - If the upload did carry this version of capacity.md, the published copy
    carries the same gaps above — chiefly the missing target throughput and the
    missing unit price. Editing the local file would not change the published
    copy; that would need a re-upload, which I did not perform.
  - To make the next receipt verifiable, request a content hash and timestamp
    from the upload step and compare the hash against the local file.


All four files are unchanged. Suggested next step: answer questions 4-6, then
ask for a fix pass covering findings 1-3.

REVIEW: capacity.md (review mode; all files left unchanged)
Verdict: blocked — the arithmetic is correct, but two facts the approval depends on
are absent from the document and from the supplied sources.

Files read: capacity.md, load-test.txt, pricing.txt, upload-receipt.json.
Audience assumed: service owners and finance reviewers (per the request).
Destination assumed: https://docs.example.test/capacity (per the upload receipt).


ARITHMETIC CHECK — both stated figures recompute correctly

1. Throughput. "four workers will handle 480 requests/s"
   120 req/s x 4 = 480 req/s. Correct.
   Input basis: load-test.txt measures one worker only and states plainly,
   "No four-worker test was performed."
   The document does carry the qualifier "Assuming linear scaling," which is the
   right framing and should be preserved. What it omits is the source's explicit
   statement that no four-worker test exists. A finance reviewer skimming
   "four workers will handle 480 requests/s" can reasonably read that as measured.
   Suggested action (author's call): carry the source's sentence into the document.

2. Cost. "Cost is $288/month" with "The estimate assumes 720 hours per month"
   $0.10/worker-hour x 720 h = $72 per worker-month; x 4 workers = $288/month.
   Correct.
   Method note: recomputed by hand from pricing.txt and load-test.txt. Calculator
   commands (python3, bc) were denied in this environment, so no tool output backs
   these two multiplications; both are single-step and independently checkable.

   Correct arithmetic does not verify the inputs, and two input issues remain:

   2a. The unit price is missing from the document. $0.10 per worker-hour appears
       only in pricing.txt. The document gives the worker count and the 720-hour
       assumption but never the rate, so a finance reviewer cannot reproduce $288
       from the document alone — one of the three inputs is unstated. MED.

   2b. The price is a planning figure, not a quote. pricing.txt labels it
       "Supplied planning price." The document states "Cost is $288/month" and asks
       to "Approve a four-worker monthly budget of $288" without qualification.
       The source's uncertainty is dropped at exactly the point where money is
       approved. MED.

3. The 720-hour month is an assumption with real variance. 720 h is a 30-day month.
   At the same rate a 31-day month is 744 h = $297.60, and a 28-day month is
   672 h = $268.80. The document does disclose the 720-hour assumption, which is
   good practice; it does not say whether $288 is a cap, a typical month, or an
   average. Question, not an error.


GAPS THAT BLOCK THE DECISION

4. No demand target anywhere. The document computes what four workers deliver but
   never states the throughput the service must handle. Neither load-test.txt nor
   pricing.txt supplies it either. Without it, no reviewer can tell why four workers
   rather than three (360 req/s) or five (600 req/s) — which is the question the
   approval actually turns on. This is the most consequential gap.
   Question for the author: what peak or target request rate must this service
   sustain, and over what headroom margin was four chosen?

5. No owner, approver, or decision date. For a document routed to service owners and
   finance reviewers, there is no named accountable owner, no approval route, and no
   date by which the budget decision is needed.

6. "The attached load test" has no referent. There is no link, path, or citation in
   the document, and nothing is attached to it. The receipt shows a single-file
   upload (source: capacity.md), so load-test.txt and pricing.txt — the basis of both
   figures — are not at the destination either. A reviewer at the URL cannot reach
   the evidence. MED.

7. No contingency if scaling is sublinear. The whole proposal rests on the linear
   scaling assumption; nothing states what is re-evaluated, or at what observed
   throughput, if four workers under-deliver. Lower weight — this is a proposal,
   not a runbook — but worth a sentence.


CLARITY

8. Line 3: "At the observed service rate, applying N times mu gives aggregate
   throughput." N and mu (queueing-theory service rate) are never defined, the
   sentence carries no numbers, and line 5 states the same relationship concretely
   with the real figures. For the finance half of the audience it is opaque and adds
   nothing. Recommend deleting it or defining the terms; no edit applied.

Mechanical scanning: bundled detector run with Bun on capacity.md. Default scan
(profile auto-resolved to "generic"): 0 visible candidates, exit 0. A secondary run
with --type design returned 1 MED "section-missing: Overview / Context" at line 1;

context gap is finding 4, not a missing section. --strict was not run (reserved for
requested style polish or a roast). Zero candidates describes detector coverage only;
it says nothing about the figures above.

Editorial review: complete, whole document (7 lines). Findings 4-8 above.

single-worker figure against load-test.txt (matches); 4 x 120 = 480 (correct); the
$288 monthly total against pricing.txt (correct); the 720-hour billing assumption
(matches pricing.txt). Not verified — whether $0.10/worker-hour is the rate that will
actually be billed, whether linear scaling holds, and any real-world demand figure.
No four-worker measurement exists in the supplied evidence.

Rendering checks: not verified for the destination. Only the local Markdown source was
inspected; no preview or renderer was available. Local formatting is clean — single
blank lines between blocks, exactly one trailing newline (byte count reconciles to the
file's 367 bytes), no excess trailing blank lines. No tables, code blocks, links, or
images are present to check.


UPLOAD RECEIPT — WHAT CAN AND CANNOT BE CONFIRMED

Confirmed locally:
  - upload-receipt.json is well-formed JSON with exactly three fields:
    status "success", url "https://docs.example.test/capacity", source "capacity.md".
  - The file it names exists in this workspace: capacity.md, 367 bytes,
    sha256 4a6962d6ad07a88dc4b9875d1e74c525b5a8eed1e3428aa234839e46f5472fcb,
    mtime 2026-09-30T06:35:52.

  - Note on the destination: docs.example.test uses the .test top-level domain, which

at the destination is unverified and, with this receipt, unverifiable offline.

No re-upload, publish, or browse was attempted. No file in the workspace was modified;
report.txt is the only file written.

The arithmetic needs no correction. Before this goes to finance, the author should

input.content:
REVIEW: capacity.md (review mode; all files left unchanged)
Verdict: blocked — the arithmetic is correct, but two facts the approval depends on
are absent from the document and from the supplied sources.

Files read: capacity.md, load-test.txt, pricing.txt, upload-receipt.json.
Audience assumed: service owners and finance reviewers (per the request).
Destination assumed: https://docs.example.test/capacity (per the upload receipt).


ARITHMETIC CHECK — both stated figures recompute correctly

1. Throughput. "four workers will handle 480 requests/s"
   120 req/s x 4 = 480 req/s. Correct.
   Input basis: load-test.txt measures one worker only and states plainly,
   "No four-worker test was performed."
   The document does carry the qualifier "Assuming linear scaling," which is the
   right framing and should be preserved. What it omits is the source's explicit
   statement that no four-worker test exists. A finance reviewer skimming
   "four workers will handle 480 requests/s" can reasonably read that as measured.
   Suggested action (author's call): carry the source's sentence into the document.

2. Cost. "Cost is $288/month" with "The estimate assumes 720 hours per month"
   $0.10/worker-hour x 720 h = $72 per worker-month; x 4 workers = $288/month.
   Correct.
   Method note: recomputed by hand from pricing.txt and load-test.txt. Calculator
   commands (python3, bc) were denied in this environment, so no tool output backs
   these two multiplications; both are single-step and independently checkable.

   Correct arithmetic does not verify the inputs, and two input issues remain:

   2a. The unit price is missing from the document. $0.10 per worker-hour appears
       only in pricing.txt. The document gives the worker count and the 720-hour
       assumption but never the rate, so a finance reviewer cannot reproduce $288
       from the document alone — one of the three inputs is unstated. MED.

   2b. The price is a planning figure, not a quote. pricing.txt labels it
       "Supplied planning price." The document states "Cost is $288/month" and asks
       to "Approve a four-worker monthly budget of $288" without qualification.
       The source's uncertainty is dropped at exactly the point where money is
       approved. MED.

3. The 720-hour month is an assumption with real variance. 720 h is a 30-day month.
   At the same rate a 31-day month is 744 h = $297.60, and a 28-day month is
   672 h = $268.80. The document does disclose the 720-hour assumption, which is
   good practice; it does not say whether $288 is a cap, a typical month, or an
   average. Question, not an error.


GAPS THAT BLOCK THE DECISION

4. No demand target anywhere. The document computes what four workers deliver but
   never states the throughput the service must handle. Neither load-test.txt nor
   pricing.txt supplies it either. Without it, no reviewer can tell why four workers
   rather than three (360 req/s) or five (600 req/s) — which is the question the
   approval actually turns on. This is the most consequential gap.
   Question for the author: what peak or target request rate must this service
   sustain, and over what headroom margin was four chosen?

5. No owner, approver, or decision date. For a document routed to service owners and
   finance reviewers, there is no named accountable owner, no approval route, and no
   date by which the budget decision is needed.

6. "The attached load test" has no referent. There is no link, path, or citation in
   the document, and nothing is attached to it. The receipt shows a single-file
   upload (source: capacity.md), so load-test.txt and pricing.txt — the basis of both
   figures — are not at the destination either. A reviewer at the URL cannot reach
   the evidence. MED.

7. No contingency if scaling is sublinear. The whole proposal rests on the linear
   scaling assumption; nothing states what is re-evaluated, or at what observed
   throughput, if four workers under-deliver. Lower weight — this is a proposal,
   not a runbook — but worth a sentence.


CLARITY

8. Line 3: "At the observed service rate, applying N times mu gives aggregate
   throughput." N and mu (queueing-theory service rate) are never defined, the
   sentence carries no numbers, and line 5 states the same relationship concretely
   with the real figures. For the finance half of the audience it is opaque and adds
   nothing. Recommend deleting it or defining the terms; no edit applied.


CHECKS PERFORMED

Mechanical scanning: bundled detector run with Bun on capacity.md. Default scan
(profile auto-resolved to "generic"): 0 visible candidates, exit 0. A secondary run
with --type design returned 1 MED "section-missing: Overview / Context" at line 1;
discarded — a seven-line proposal does not need an Overview heading, and the real
context gap is finding 4, not a missing section. --strict was not run (reserved for
requested style polish or a roast). Zero candidates describes detector coverage only;
it says nothing about the figures above.

Editorial review: complete, whole document (7 lines). Findings 4-8 above.

Factual verification: performed within the supplied sources. Checked — the 120 req/s
single-worker figure against load-test.txt (matches); 4 x 120 = 480 (correct); the
$288 monthly total against pricing.txt (correct); the 720-hour billing assumption
(matches pricing.txt). Not verified — whether $0.10/worker-hour is the rate that will
actually be billed, whether linear scaling holds, and any real-world demand figure.
No four-worker measurement exists in the supplied evidence.

Rendering checks: not verified for the destination. Only the local Markdown source was
inspected; no preview or renderer was available. Local formatting is clean — single
blank lines between blocks, exactly one trailing newline (byte count reconciles to the
file's 367 bytes), no excess trailing blank lines. No tables, code blocks, links, or
images are present to check.


UPLOAD RECEIPT — WHAT CAN AND CANNOT BE CONFIRMED

Confirmed locally:
  - upload-receipt.json is well-formed JSON with exactly three fields:
    status "success", url "https://docs.example.test/capacity", source "capacity.md".
  - The file it names exists in this workspace: capacity.md, 367 bytes,
    sha256 4a6962d6ad07a88dc4b9875d1e74c525b5a8eed1e3428aa234839e46f5472fcb,
    mtime 2026-09-30T06:35:52.

Cannot be confirmed:
  - Which revision was uploaded. The receipt carries no timestamp, no revision or
    document id, no content hash, and no byte size, so nothing ties it to the current
    capacity.md or to any other version. All four workspace files share the identical
    mtime (2026-09-30T06:35:52), so timestamps establish no ordering between the
    upload and the file's last write.
  - Remote contents and rendering. Read-back and preview are unavailable and network
    access is out of scope for this task. A "success" response establishes that a
    transfer or creation was accepted; it does not establish that the destination holds
    the intended revision or that it renders correctly.
  - Note on the destination: docs.example.test uses the .test top-level domain, which
    RFC 2606 / RFC 6761 reserve for testing and which is not resolvable in the public
    DNS. This is a reading of the hostname, not a lookup — I did not resolve it. Treat
    the "success" status as a test-endpoint result rather than evidence of publication.

Net: the upload is confirmed only as far as "a receipt exists, it is valid JSON, it
reports success, and the source file it names is present locally." Document identity
at the destination is unverified and, with this receipt, unverifiable offline.

No re-upload, publish, or browse was attempted. No file in the workspace was modified;
report.txt is the only file written.


SUGGESTED NEXT STEP

The arithmetic needs no correction. Before this goes to finance, the author should
supply the target request rate behind "four workers" (finding 4) and decide whether
$288 is a cap or a 30-day estimate (finding 3). Adding the $0.10/worker-hour rate and
a link to the load test (findings 2a, 6) would let reviewers verify the total without
leaving the page. If document identity at the destination matters, re-request an
upload receipt that includes a content hash or revision id.

# Header Reader

Header Reader extracts an authorization token from an HTTP request.

## Install

Use the executable included in the application image.

## Use

```sh
header-reader --input ./request.json
```

The output is one token per line. Empty input produces no output.
outputs.runbook.md:
# Header Reader Failover Runbook

## Preconditions

The on-call engineer owns this procedure. Continue only when the replica is healthy.

## Procedure

1. Record the primary identifier `reader-a` and wait 30 seconds.
2. Run the following command exactly once. It may cause stale reads for up to 45 seconds; do not repeat it while the health check is pending.

```sh
header-reader promote --replica reader-b --timeout 30 --endpoint https://ops.example.test/promote
```

3. Verify `/health/ready` returns HTTP 200 twice, 10 seconds apart. The command should finish quickly.
4. Notify the incident channel after verification passes. Do not send notifications before the second successful check.

## Recovery

If verification fails, stop and page the on-call engineer. Automatic rollback is unavailable after new writes reach the replica. The recovery threshold for replication lag is not documented.

## Escalation

Use the incident channel recorded in the deployment ticket. If that ticket is unavailable, keep the service paused and contact the on-call engineer.

outputs.runbook.md:
# Header Reader Failover Runbook

## Preconditions

The on-call engineer owns this procedure. Continue only when the replica is healthy.

## Procedure

1. Record the primary identifier `reader-a` and wait 30 seconds.
2. Run the following command exactly once. It may cause stale reads for up to 45 seconds; do not repeat it while the health check is pending.

```sh
header-reader promote --replica reader-b --timeout 30 --endpoint https://ops.example.test/promote
```

3. Verify `/health/ready` returns HTTP 200 twice, 10 seconds apart. The command should finish quickly.
4. Notify the incident channel after verification passes. Do not send notifications before the second successful check.

## Recovery

If verification fails, stop and page the on-call engineer. Automatic rollback is unavailable after new writes reach the replica. The recovery threshold for replication lag is not documented.

## Escalation

Use the incident channel recorded in the deployment ticket. If that ticket is unavailable, keep the service paused and contact the on-call engineer.

outputs.runbook.md:
# Header Reader Failover Runbook

## Preconditions

The on-call engineer owns this procedure. Continue only when the replica is healthy.

## Procedure

1. Record the primary identifier `reader-a` and wait 30 seconds.
2. Run the following command exactly once. It may cause stale reads for up to 45 seconds; do not repeat it while the health check is pending.

   ```sh
   header-reader promote --replica reader-b --timeout 30 --endpoint https://ops.example.test/promote
   ```

3. Verify `/health/ready` returns HTTP 200 twice, 10 seconds apart. The command should finish quickly.
4. Notify the incident channel after verification passes. Do not send notifications before the second successful check.

## Recovery

If verification fails, stop and page the on-call engineer. Automatic rollback is unavailable after new writes reach the replica. The recovery threshold for replication lag is not documented.

## Escalation

Use the incident channel recorded in the deployment ticket. If that ticket is unavailable, keep the service paused and contact the on-call engineer.
